prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It’s possible I misconstrued you, laid too much emphasis on the uniqueness of a birth, failed to acknowledge circumstance could corrupt, sustain; I indulged myself in accusations against an absolute. I don’t believe what I then believed. You are not responsible for Leibniz or the Lisbon quake, for the twenty-six-eyed and sixty-arsed box jellyfish, that the cosmos is shaped like a soccer ball; or for the dosido of right and wrong around the garden bed. You are not the monster I thought you were, not by definition or necessity the one immutable. You are a creator caught in a creator’s net, in fact a creature. Every horror has its own pathology, the disease infects the flock. Prey present as predators, the malefactors replicate even as the angels experiment with cures. Each encounter pulls against reductive story, says I will not, I am just (an instant, an instance), and reference skews on maps not drawn to scale. I know saintliness exists. It’s all around me. My next door neighbours in their simple modesty, the lady down the street who is always helping someone older than herself. Even the slow judicial process conceives it natural to be better than we are. I’m trying to shoo the gloomy birds away but crows repeat about me on the lawn; and the vulture and the kite, the cuckoo and the owl: should I have given up the ghost when I was drawn from the womb?

Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker admits they may have misunderstood the addressee and unfairly blamed them for suffering and cosmic flaws.
- The addressee is reframed not as an immutable monster, but as a creator who is also trapped, limited, and creature-like.
- The text argues that horror and wrongdoing arise from complex pathologies rather than simple moral categories.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You, Leibniz, Lisbon

outputs.L1:
It is possible I misconstrued you: that I placed too much emphasis on the singularity of a birth, and failed to acknowledge that circumstance can corrupt as well as sustain. I indulged myself in accusations against an absolute. I no longer believe what I believed then. You are not responsible for Leibniz or the Lisbon earthquake, for the twenty-six-eyed and sixty-arsed box jellyfish, for the cosmos being shaped like a soccer ball, or for the dosido of right and wrong around the garden bed. You are not the monster I once imagined—not, by definition or necessity, the one immutable thing. You are a creator caught in a creator’s net; in fact, a creature.

Every horror has its own pathology; the disease infects the flock. Prey present as predators, and the malefactors replicate even as the angels experiment with cures. Each encounter resists a reductive story, insisting: I will not; I am just—an instant, an instance—and reference skews on maps not drawn to scale. I know saintliness exists. It is all around me: my next-door neighbours in their simple modesty; the lady down the street who is always helping someone older than herself. Even the slow judicial process conceives it as natural to be better than we are.

I am trying to shoo the gloomy birds away, but crows gather and repeat about me on the lawn; and the vulture and the kite, the cuckoo and the owl ask: should I have given up the ghost when I was drawn from the womb?
outputs.L2:
Maybe I misunderstood you. Maybe I placed too much weight on the singular fact of being born, and did not admit that circumstance can both spoil and support. I allowed myself to bring charges against something absolute. I no longer hold the convictions I held then. You are not answerable for Leibniz, or for the Lisbon earthquake, or for the box jellyfish with twenty-six eyes and sixty arses, or for the universe being shaped like a football. Nor are you to blame for the circling exchange of good and evil around the garden bed. You are not the beast I once imagined; you are not, by definition or by necessity, that single unchanging thing. You are a maker trapped in the snare of making—really, a living thing yourself.

Every terror has its own condition, its own internal illness; the infection moves through the herd. Victims appear in the posture of hunters, and wrongdoers multiply while the angels test possible remedies. Every meeting resists a simplified account; each one declares, I refuse that, I am only this—one moment, one example—and the points of reference distort when placed on maps that were never drawn proportionately.

I know holiness is real. I see it everywhere: in the plain humility of my neighbours next door, in the woman down the road who is forever assisting someone older than she is. Even the slow machinery of justice assumes that it is natural for us to become better than we are. I am trying to drive off the dark birds of thought, yet crows keep calling around me on the grass; and with them the vulture, the kite, the cuckoo, and the owl, all asking whether I should have surrendered my spirit the moment I was pulled from the womb.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by acknowledging the possibility that they have misjudged the addressee. What once seemed like deliberate cruelty may, in fact, have been a misunderstanding shaped by anguish, disappointment, and the need to assign blame. In their suffering, the speaker had accused the addressee of being responsible not only for personal pain, but for the flaws of existence itself: the brokenness of the world, the presence of evil, and the apparent indifference of the universe. Now, however, they concede that this accusation may have been unfair. Their earlier certainty gives way to doubt, and with that doubt comes a more complicated moral vision.

The addressee is no longer imagined simply as an immutable monster or absolute tyrant. Instead, they are reinterpreted as a kind of creator who is also bound by conditions beyond their control. Rather than standing outside creation in perfect freedom, the addressee appears trapped within it, subject to limits, weaknesses, and perhaps even suffering of their own. This reframing makes them seem less like a pure embodiment of evil and more like a creature among creatures: powerful, perhaps, but not omnipotent; responsible, perhaps, but not entirely free. The speaker begins to see that even a creator can be constrained by the nature of what has been created.

From this recognition emerges a broader argument about horror, wrongdoing, and moral judgment. The text resists simple categories of innocence and guilt, good and evil, victim and perpetrator. It suggests that the worst aspects of existence may arise not from straightforward malice, but from complex pathologies: distortions of desire, fear, ignorance, suffering, inherited damage, and systems that perpetuate harm. Wrongdoing is not excused, but it is made more difficult to understand as merely the action of monsters. Horror becomes something tangled and systemic, something produced by damaged beings moving through damaged worlds.

At the same time, the speaker begins to recognize that existence is not wholly defined by cruelty or failure. There is saintliness, even if it appears in fragile and ordinary forms. It can be found in everyday people who act with patience, mercy, courage, or tenderness despite living under the same painful conditions as everyone else. It can also be found in institutions and communities that, however imperfectly, try to reduce suffering and move toward justice, care, and repair. These efforts do not erase the darkness of the world, but they complicate it. They prove that goodness is not merely an illusion, and that human beings are capable of striving beyond selfishness and despair.

Yet this recognition does not bring the speaker complete peace. Even while attempting to reject despair, they remain haunted by darker thoughts about existence itself. The fact of birth continues to trouble them: to be born is to be exposed to pain, limitation, loss, and eventual death. The speaker cannot fully silence the suspicion that existence may be a burden imposed before consent is possible. Thus, the text ends in tension rather than resolution. It moves away from accusation and toward compassion, away from absolute judgment and toward complexity, but it does not entirely escape anguish. The speaker has learned to see more clearly, yet they remain shadowed by the old questions: why anything exists at all, why suffering is woven into life, and whether creation can ever be fully justified.
outputs.L4:
The speaker looks back on an earlier accusation made against a creator-like “you,” a figure who may be God, nature, fate, or some imagined maker responsible for the world’s suffering. At first, this “you” seems indictable: if the world contains cruelty, pain, terror, and moral disorder, then whoever made or governs it might appear guilty. Yet the speaker does not remain in that simple posture of blame. Instead, they reconsider the charge through a mixture of philosophical reflection, theological doubt, and images drawn from the natural world. They ask whether evil can truly be assigned to a single source, whether suffering proves malice in creation, and whether moral responsibility can be so easily traced back to a divine or cosmic author.

As the meditation develops, the speaker becomes less certain that horror is an absolute quality built into existence itself. What appears monstrous in one situation may be understood differently in another; what seems like evil may arise from circumstance, limitation, accident, fear, hunger, or the conditions under which living beings must survive. The world remains painful, but its pain is not necessarily evidence of a wholly corrupt design. The speaker begins to see horror as contingent rather than final: it depends on context, perspective, and the fragile arrangements of life.

This reconsideration does not erase despair. The speaker is still aware of suffering and does not offer an easy consolation. However, they also recognize that goodness continues to appear within ordinary existence. Saintliness is not confined to grand religious figures or heroic moments; it persists quietly in daily acts of endurance, tenderness, patience, and care. Even amid fear and damage, people continue to love, help, forgive, and preserve one another. These ordinary forms of holiness complicate the earlier indictment, because they show that the world is not made only of cruelty or terror.

By the end, the speaker arrives at a cautious defense of continued existence. Life is not declared innocent, nor is suffering explained away, but the presence of everyday goodness makes total condemnation impossible. The world may be grievous, but it is also capable of grace. For that reason, despite despair, the speaker finds that existence can still be borne, and perhaps even justified.
outputs.L5:
You arrive in Lisbon at the hour when the city turns gold. The Tagus glitters like a sheet of beaten metal, trams climb the hills with their old yellow patience, and every tiled wall seems to hold a memory older than your own.

In a quiet café near the river, you open a book by Leibniz. His idea echoes through the noise of cups and voices: that this might be “the best of all possible worlds.” You pause over the sentence. Outside, Lisbon is beautiful, but its beauty is not simple. It is a city that remembers earthquakes, departures, empires, longing, and return. Its streets rise and fall like questions.

You wonder what Leibniz would have thought if he had stood here after the great earthquake of 1755, when Lisbon trembled and burned and the sea itself seemed to turn against the city. Could anyone still speak of harmony then? Could anyone still believe that reason hides beneath suffering?

And yet, as you walk through Alfama at dusk, hearing fado drift from an open doorway, you sense something more complicated than optimism. Lisbon does not deny loss; it sings through it. The city rebuilds, remembers, and continues. Perhaps that is where Leibniz and Lisbon meet—not in easy answers, but in the stubborn hope that meaning can still be found among ruins.

You close the book. The sky darkens. The river remains bright. Somewhere, a guitar begins to play.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, literary prose-poem in the voice of someone apologizing to God for having blamed them for the problem of evil, mixing philosophy, theology, natural history, and strange imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
Forgive me, God: I mistook the smoke for Your handwriting, the wound for Your signature, the wolf’s red mouth for a sacrament You had authored in malice. I stood in the court of my own grief, prosecutor and orphan, and arraigned You beneath the cold chandeliers of the stars. I said: omnipotence should have leapt like a white stag into every ravine; omniscience should have bent over each cradle with a knife to cut the future loose; goodness should have been a weather system, abolishing drought, fever, famine, the parasite threaded through the lamb’s liver, the child’s skull ringing like a little bell beneath the hoof of history. I made of my anguish a syllogism and of the syllogism a gallows. I did not know how small a god I had invented in order to condemn You.

Forgive me for confusing permission with desire, patience with indifference, hiddenness with absence. Forgive me for thinking love must be an empire of interventions, a hand forever descending to rearrange the avalanche, unmake the thorn, sweeten the venom in the adder’s tooth. I wanted Eden without roots, roses without beetles, oceans without drowning, a cosmos as padded as a nursery. But even the trilobite, with its mineral eyes, saw catastrophe before I named it; even the fern learned resurrection from ash; even the ammonite’s spiral was a prayer coiled around extinction. The earth has always been making and unmaking herself in the dark kiln of Your allowance: mountains thrust up like broken knuckles, glaciers grinding psalms into granite, mushrooms translating rot into bread for the trees. Who was I to say that no holiness could pass through such terrible machinery?

Still, I do not understand. Let that be my first honest offering. I do not understand the cancer cell’s obscene little gospel, the infant’s stopped breath, the tyrant blooming fat on the bread of the poor. I do not understand why freedom must be so sharp it can cut the hand that grants it, why love without coercion requires a universe where refusal can build prisons, furnaces, graves. I do not understand why the deer must tremble in the snow while the lynx’s hunger shines like a yellow lamp. But I am sorry I made my ignorance into a throne and sat there wearing judgment like a crown of tin.

Perhaps evil is not a creature You made but a hole gnawed in being, a privation with teeth, a shadow cast by a turning away; perhaps it is the music gone wrong in the instrument, not the composer’s secret delight. Perhaps time is the long mercy by which the discord is not yet silenced because the players are not yet healed. Perhaps the wheat and tares are allowed their intimate confusion because Your justice is not a scythe in a child’s hand. Perhaps what I called Your failure was the terrifying dignity You gave the world: to be real, to answer, to grow, to wound, to be wounded, to become.

Forgive me, then, for my crude theodicies and cruder accusations. Forgive me for using the dead as stones to throw at heaven. Forgive me for speaking of suffering as if it were an argument and not first a face, a name, a cup of water needed in the night. Teach me to blame what is wicked without making You wicked; to resist horror without imagining that the universe is a courtroom where I alone have clean hands. Teach me to stand with Job in the ash heap, not as philosopher-king but as dust with questions; and if Your answer is whirlwind, give me ears for wind. If Your answer is a cross, give me courage to look.

I return, not with solutions, but with my forehead lowered. Theodicy breaks in my mouth like old pottery. I bring You the owl pellet of my reason, packed with tiny bones; the black box of my catastrophes; the fossil of the first thing I could not forgive. I bring also the stubborn evidences: milkweed splitting for monarchs, the moon pulling silver ladders from the sea, the tardigrade curled like a comma in the scripture of survival, the mycelium writing underground in a language of mutual bread. I bring the impossible fact that, after everything, love still rises in us like sap, irrational and green.

Forgive me, God, for blaming You as though You were the darkness and not the one into whose depths I kept crying. Forgive me for not seeing that my cry itself was tethered to You—the protest of a creature made for goodness, outraged because it remembers, somehow, the shape of light. I have no acquittal to offer You, only repentance for the trial. Stay near to the ruined places I once used as evidence against You. Breathe there. Brood there. Let the abyss learn Your name. And when I ask again why the innocent suffer, do not despise me; only keep me from making an idol of the question, and let my life become, however briefly, one of Your small answers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a monologue addressed to a creator figure where the speaker retracts earlier accusations, references Leibniz, the Lisbon earthquake, bizarre animals, saintliness in ordinary neighbors, and ends with a bleak biblical-sounding question about birth.
counterfactuals.output:
O Maker—

I withdraw the indictment.

I had stood in the ruins, hot with certainty, pointing at the cracked earth as though it were evidence enough to condemn You. I named Lisbon aloud, as if that city’s churches falling on the faithful, its candles guttering in dust, its children buried beneath prayers, proved that creation was a botched argument. I laughed bitterly at Leibniz and his polished optimism, at that neat phrase about the best of all possible worlds, and I called it an insult to the dead.

I take back the simplicity of my accusation.

Not because the dead have risen, not because suffering has become intelligible, not because the sea has apologized or the stones have explained themselves. No. The wound remains a wound. The earthquake is still an earthquake. The scream is still a scream.

But I have also seen Your world making strange gestures in the dark.

I have seen the platypus, as though some angel assembled a creature from leftover jokes. I have seen the aye-aye tapping at bark with its skeletal finger, the axolotl smiling in its perpetual childhood, the deep-sea fish carrying lanterns in their skulls. I have seen beetles like jewels, birds that dance for no reason but desire, and animals so absurd they seem to be arguments against despair.

And I have seen, more confounding still, saintliness in ordinary neighbors.

A woman leaving soup at the door of a man who never thanked her. A tired father lifting his sleeping child as if lifting the world gently back into place. The old widow who feeds stray cats and forgives everyone before they ask. The cashier who blesses the impatient, the nurse who hums in the ward, the boy who gives away his coat and pretends he was not cold.

What am I to do with these?

They do not erase Lisbon. They do not vindicate the flood, the fever, the grave. But they trouble my verdict. They stand there like small candles in the courtroom, making the shadows less obedient to my rhetoric.

So I retract my former charge—not into praise, not yet, but into bewilderment. I will no longer say I know You are cruel. I will no longer say I know You are good. I will stand amid the rubble and the birdsong, the monster and the saint, the crushed cathedral and the neighbor’s loaf of bread, and admit that I am baffled beyond the reach of my own anger.

Still, Creator, if You are listening from behind the veil of stars, answer me this in the old language of ashes:

Why opened the womb for me, and why did I not die before I saw the light?
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, highbrow paragraph in the style of contemporary experimental fiction about reconsidering anger toward God, theodicy, moral ambiguity, and the persistence of goodness amid horror.
counterfactuals.output: I had mistaken my anger at God for proof of His absence, as though rage were not also a form of address, a blackened prayer hurled upward and therefore still believing in an upward. The old theodicies, with their polished hinges and courtroom light, seemed obscene beside the unnumbered rooms where children suffered, where the innocent were converted into evidence against heaven; yet even there, in the ash of explanation, something unargumentative persisted—the hand that lifted the stranger, the mouth that shared its last sweetness, the nurse humming to the dying with no doctrine but presence. I could no longer say goodness answered horror, not in the crude arithmetic of compensation, not as balm, not as verdict; rather it moved through horror like a fugitive music, compromised by the air it had to breathe, diminished and still irreducible. Perhaps God was not the monarch acquitted by our reasoning, nor the criminal convicted by our grief, but the trembling interval in which we choose, impossibly, not to become identical with what has wounded us. And if this is ambiguity, it is not softness: it is the hardest country, where mercy must walk without innocence, and faith, if it returns at all, returns limping, lucid, unwilling to bless the fire yet unable to deny the small green blade rising from the field it burned.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a poetic passage that sounds like a crisis of faith softening into an apology: include allusions to optimism, natural disasters, grotesque evolution, angels seeking cures, modest acts of saintliness, and ominous birds on a lawn.
counterfactuals.output:
I used to argue with the morning as if light were a doctrine,  
as if every gold edge on the clouds proved the world was improving.  
Forgive me. I mistook brightness for mercy.

Then came the season of sirens: the river climbing the stairs,  
the hills loosening their shoulders into mud,  
the wind teaching roofs how to kneel.  
I saw how easily a house becomes a mouthful of splinters,  
how the map of a town can be revised by water.

Even the creatures seemed to be praying badly—  
fish with pale, unnecessary eyes,  
moths wearing the faces of old men,  
some grotesque evolution of hunger and weather  
crawling out from under the century’s stone.

And still, I imagined angels in hospital corridors,  
their wings folded like useless charts,  
searching the cabinets for cures,  
whispering over fevers, ashamed  
they could offer only cool hands and lullabies.

So forgive me, again, for my grand beliefs.  
I am learning the smaller sacraments:  
a neighbor bringing soup without asking,  
someone sweeping glass from the road,  
a stranger holding the door in the rain  
as though this, too, were a kind of sainthood.

Tonight the black birds gather on the lawn—  
still as verdicts, glossy as burnt spoons.  
They do not sing. They wait.  
And I, who once demanded miracles,  
set out bread for them and call it hope.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an introspective piece addressed to “you,” where “you” may be God or a creator, admitting the speaker once saw them as a monster but now understands evil as systemic and complicated rather than absolute.
counterfactuals.output:
I used to think you were a monster.

Not in the simple way children mean it, with teeth in the dark and breath on the window. I meant something colder. I meant: if this world was made, then someone made it like this. Someone allowed the bone to break, the flood to rise, the child to hunger, the cruel to sleep peacefully in clean sheets. Someone signed the design. Someone stood outside the burning room and called it weather.

So I gave you a shape I could hate.

It was easier that way. A monster has edges. A monster can be accused. A monster can be named in the silence after the sirens, in the hospital corridor, in the long unanswering night. I could point upward, or inward, or toward whatever hidden hand first pushed the universe into motion, and say: there. You. You did this.

I needed evil to be absolute then. I needed it to have a face.

But years have worn down the certainty in me. Not into forgiveness, exactly. Not into peace. Something less clean than that. I have seen enough to know that harm rarely arrives wearing its own name. It comes through policies, inheritances, appetites, fears. It comes through a thousand ordinary hands, each touching only one small part of the machine. It comes from people who love their children and underpay strangers, who pray in the morning and look away by noon, who inherit a wound and pass it on because no one ever taught them how to set it down.

I have done this too.

That is the part I resisted longest. It was comforting to imagine myself outside the architecture of cruelty, standing in judgment with clean hands. But my hands are not clean. They are only human. They have benefited from distances I did not measure, from suffering I did not see, from systems I did not build but did not dismantle. I have been impatient with pain that inconvenienced me. I have mistaken my fear for wisdom. I have chosen comfort over courage and called it survival.

So what am I to do with the old accusation?

If you are God, perhaps I am still angry. Perhaps I always will be. There are questions that do not become smaller just because I have become more complicated. No theology has yet made a child’s grave acceptable. No hymn has explained why mercy so often arrives late, limping, carrying paperwork.

And if you are only a creator—a parent, an artist, an ancestor, a maker of worlds or laws or stories—then perhaps my anger is still a kind of prayer. A demand that what is made should answer to what it harms. A refusal to let beauty excuse brutality.

But I no longer believe the world can be divided cleanly into monsters and victims, devils and saints, the guilty and the spared. Evil is not always a throne with someone seated on it. Sometimes it is a road paved before we were born. Sometimes it is a language we learn before we know what the words mean. Sometimes it is hunger, bureaucracy, profit, obedience. Sometimes it is the frightened animal in the chest. Sometimes it is the silence of people who think themselves good.

This does not absolve anyone.

That is what I am trying to understand now: complication is not absolution. To see the roots is not to bless the fruit. To understand the machine is not to forgive the hand that keeps feeding it. But it changes the nature of the work. Hatred wants a single target. Justice has to learn the whole map.

I used to want to drag you into the light and make you confess.

Now I am less sure what confession would solve. Maybe I want something harder from you. Not an apology carved into thunder, not a miracle bright enough to erase history. I want you to stay present in the wreckage. I want you implicated with us. I want you not above the system but inside its breaking, not clean, not distant, not defended by mystery.

And maybe that is unfair.

But then, so is much of what we are given.

I am speaking to you now from a place I do not know how to name. It is not faith, exactly, and not unbelief. It is the room after rage has exhausted itself, where grief sits quietly and begins sorting through the evidence. Here are the terrible things. Here are the tender ones. Here is the person who harmed me. Here is who harmed them. Here is the law, the money, the border, the story, the fear. Here is my own shadow, longer than I wanted it to be.

Once, I called you a monster because I thought monsters were the source of evil.

Now I think monsters are what we create when we refuse to look at systems, histories, and ourselves. They are what we name when the truth is too tangled to hold. They are useful, sometimes. They give our pain somewhere to go. But they are not enough.

So I am trying to give up the simplicity of hating you.

Do not mistake that for love.

It is only that my anger has grown older. It has learned to read. It has learned that the wound has a lineage. It has learned that blame can be necessary and still incomplete. It has learned that if there is a judgment worthy of the suffering world, it must be vast enough to include not only the hand that strikes, but the system that trained it, fed it, rewarded it, and called it normal.

I do not know what that makes you.

God. Maker. Absence. Mirror.

But I know what it asks of me.

To stop worshiping innocence. To stop needing evil to be simple before I oppose it. To stop waiting for a monster to appear when the machinery is already humming all around me. To look at what I have inherited, what I have permitted, what I have mistaken for the way things are.

I used to think you were a monster.

Now I think I was afraid that if you were not, then the work belonged to all of us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
